beats.script_body: After serving in World War II, Korea, and Vietnam, the aircraft carrier U.S.S. Intrepid found a permanent home alongside Pier 86 on the Hudson River, where it metamorphosed from a fighting machine into a museum of mankind's achievements on water, in the air, and in outer space. On the flight deck you can relive the infamous day in 1944 when the carrier survived direct hits by two Japanese kamikaze planes.

beats.source_passage: After serving in World War II, Korea, and Vietnam, the U.S.S. Intrepid (CVS-11) found a permanent home alongside Pier 86 on the Hudson River. Here it metamorphosed from a fighting machine into a wide-ranging museum devoted to mankind's achievements on the water, in the air, and even in outer space. ... relive the infamous day in 1944 when the carrier survived direct hits by two Japanese kamikaze planes.

beats.script_body: The space exhibits aboard Intrepid may seem out of place on a warship, but they are deeply relevant: the carrier served as the recovery ship on several Mercury and Gemini space missions, plucking returning astronauts and capsules from the ocean. Among the aircraft crowding the flight deck is a supersonic Concorde, and you can test your skills in an A-6 fighter-jet flight simulator.

beats.script_body: Gazing up at the neon-lit billboards and theater marquees as a current of pedestrians and traffic swirls by, you feel the overwhelming sense that Times Square really is the 'Crossroads of the World.' More than a million people gather here each New Year's Eve to watch the Waterford crystal ball on the One Times Square skyscraper mark the start of a new year.

beats.script_body: It's hard to imagine now, but the square was once the outer edge of civilization — a collection of liveries and stables where many New Yorkers kept their horses and buggies. By the end of the 19th century the first theaters had begun to appear, and by the early 20th century this stretch of Broadway had been dubbed the Great White Way, after its brilliant lighting.

beats.script_body: Oil fortune heir John D. Rockefeller, Jr., hatched the idea of a grand cultural, commercial, and entertainment complex on a large Midtown property he was leasing from Columbia University. The task of creating this 'city within a city' was handed to Wallace K. Harrison, whose team helped construct nineteen buildings, ranging from immensely tall to surprisingly short, fronted by a plaza that would become a New York icon in its own right. The center's 'front door' is on Fifth Avenue, with the stubby Maison Française on the left and a mirror-image British Empire edifice on the right; the flower-filled Channel Gardens in between provide a route into the heart of the center, culminating in Rockefeller Plaza. Soaring straight up from the plaza, the seventy-story General Electric Building reflects both the art deco vibe of the 1930s, when most of Rockefeller Center was built, and the boxy modernism of the postwar period. Affectionately called '30 Rock' by those who work within, the skyscraper was originally home to the Radio Corporation of America, RKO Pictures, and NBC television, and its lobby flaunts massive murals by Spanish artist José Maria Sert.

beats.script_body: A few discerning women collectors, including Lillie P. Bliss and Abby Aldrich Rockefeller, founded MoMA in 1929. Today it holds more than 150,000 pieces of art as well as 22,000 film, video, and media works. The current building opened in 2004, its six floors nearly doubling the exhibition space, though the permanent collection still has to be shown in rotating displays.

beats.script_body: The fourth floor displays the major figures of abstract expressionism. Jackson Pollock's classic 'drip' painting 'One: Number 31, 1950' was created with the canvas laid out on the floor, while Latvian-born Mark Rothko painted large, hypnotic canvases of solid-color rectangles, such as 'No. 3/No. 13' from 1949. Pop Art reflected the consumerism of the 1950s and '60s through mass-media imagery, as in Andy Warhol's 'Campbell's Soup Cans' of 1962 and Roy Lichtenstein's 'Drowning Girl' of 1963, which carries the melodrama of a comic-strip frame.

beats.script_body: Also on the fifth floor is surrealist Salvador Dali's masterpiece 'The Persistence of Memory.' Dali drew inspiration from an overripe Camembert cheese to depict the melting watches in the painting. Nearby, in 'Broadway Boogie Woogie,' Dutch artist Piet Mondrian combined his trademark grid with tiny squares and rectangles of color, suggesting the fast tempo of New York and his interest in jazz.

beats.script_body: The seat of New York's Roman Catholic archdiocese and one of the nation's most renowned churches, St. Patrick's is a tribute to the Irish Americans who played such an integral role in New York's history, and to the can-do spirit of the nineteenth-century archbishop John Hughes. Ignoring criticism from wealthy patrons and poor parishioners alike, Hughes launched the project shortly before the Civil War on a patch of land that then lay well outside the city center. Architect James Renwick patterned the massive neo-Gothic structure after Germany's Cologne Cathedral. Although the church was consecrated in 1879, construction continued through the turn of the twentieth century. Its twin spires were the tallest landmark along Fifth Avenue until the early 1930s, when skyscrapers overtook the neighborhood. The 108-foot-high nave can seat 2,500 people, and a number of its exceptionally rich stained-glass windows were made in Chartres, France.

beats.script_body: A masterpiece of beaux arts design, this steel, granite, and limestone building opened in 1913 as the city's state-of-the-art train depot. Outside, beneath the massive central window, a statue commemorates railroad tycoon Cornelius Vanderbilt. In the Main Concourse the vaulted ceiling is decorated with the constellations of the zodiac, and as light streams through the cast-iron windows and shadows move across the Tennessee marble floor, the space looks more like an ancient temple than a hub for transportation.

beats.script_body: Art deco's fusion of the utilitarian with the artistic reaches its peak in the Chrysler Building. Automobile magnate Walter P. Chrysler funded the structure himself, working closely with architect William Van Alen. Although the 1,050-foot building kept its 'world's tallest' tag for only a year, its artistic merit has continued to soar. Many of Van Alen's details were inspired by car motifs, including the stainless steel gargoyles modeled after the radiator caps of a 1929 Chrysler. The building is best viewed from the Empire State Building's observation deck, but visitors can also explore the art deco lobby, once a Chrysler showroom.

beats.script_body: A standout along this part of the East River, the United Nations complex still looks as modern today as it did upon its completion in 1952. American architect Wallace K. Harrison had overall design control, but consulted other maestros including Brazil's Oscar Niemeyer and France's Le Corbusier, who devised the winning plan. The 39-story Secretariat Building dominates the complex, and directly below it sits the futuristic General Assembly building with its swayback roof and trademark dome. Guided tours start from the Public Lobby of the General Assembly building.

beats.script_body: The robust lines and soaring spires of the Chrysler and Empire State Buildings epitomize New York's love affair in the 1920s and '30s with the streamlined design of art deco. The style acquired official recognition at a 1925 exhibition in Paris, the 'Exposition Internationale des Arts Décoratifs,' and the shorthand term 'art deco' stuck. Its sunbursts, chevrons, zigzags, and other geometric patterns could be applied to diners and jewelry, elevators and comic books, planes, trains, and automobiles, and New York transformed itself into a science-fiction metropolis of silvery skyscrapers.

beats.script_body: Art deco also solved a problem introduced by the 1916 Zoning Resolution, which required buildings to be 'stepped up' to the sky so a modicum of sunlight could reach the streets below. Art deco gave these setbacks a decorative purpose, most brilliantly in the stepped spire of the Chrysler Building.

beats.script_body: Every holiday season a towering Norway spruce graces Rockefeller Center. The tree, which averages about 80 feet high, is dressed with more than five miles of lights and topped with a Swarovski crystal star. At the nationally broadcast lighting ceremony, usually held in late November, a lineup of singers and celebrities launches the festive season with carols as thousands fill the sidewalks to watch.

beats.source_passage: Every holiday season, a towering Norway spruce graces Rockefeller Center (see pp. 92-93). The tree, which averages about 80 feet (24 m) high, is dressed with more than 5 miles (8 km) of lights and a Swarovski crystal star at the top. At the nationally broadcast lighting ceremony, usually held in late November, a lineup of singers and celebrities launches the festive season with carols and performances, as thousands fill the sidewalks to watch.
